ITM750 · Academic project

Planning and Controlling an IT Project from Schedule to Handover

Adnan Khan

I used Microsoft Project for individual scheduling and resource assignments, then worked with my team on a complete Online Ministry of Labour Services (OMLS) planning case. This version covers the whole proposal: services, requirements, scope, stakeholders, integration, schedule, budget, risk and handover.

Tools and environment

Microsoft Project; working calendars; Gantt charts; resource and cost planning; project charter; stakeholder register; communications planning; earned value and risk analysis.

Individual plans: Adnan Khan. OMLS team: Adnan Khan - charter/stakeholders; Abesan Vijayabalan - background/communications; Wamiq Khan - processes/risk; Akash Wahi - requirements/time; Vishal Sambhwani - integration/cost. February-March 2026.

Build an individual schedule

I set the working calendar, established the project start and organised tasks into initiation, planning, design, implementation and closing. Predecessors and milestones make the sequence visible. The Gantt view provides a time-based check against the task list.

Assign resources and interpret the estimate

I attached work and material resources, entered availability and rates, and reviewed the cost mix. The individual plan records 105 days, 1,696 work hours and CAD 1,066,464. Material costs of CAD 1,009,400 and work costs of CAD 57,064 reconcile to the total.

  • I also inspected phase and time-based work/cost reports. These are planning quantities, not completed effort or expenditure.

Define the complete OMLS service proposal

Our team proposed a central web portal and approximately 300 public kiosks to improve access to labour-related services. The model routes kiosk requests through local LANs and regional servers to headquarters in Toronto. Social channels provide information and links; account-based transactions belong on the portal.

  • Service coverage: employment standards; workplace health and safety; labour relations; job-seeker support; employer support; immigration/settlement; education and careers.
  • The proposal includes bilingual public interfaces and clearing kiosk session data.

Turn requirements into scope and deliverables

Our requirements cover searching, information retrieval, web/kiosk access and integration between regional and central systems. My charter connects these needs to analysis, design, development, testing, a ten-kiosk pilot, rollout, training and handover. Policy changes and ongoing post-project maintenance are outside the stated project scope.

  • Quality requirements include usability, accessibility, security, reliability, interoperability and scalability.
  • Acceptance would need checks for session clearing, authenticated actions and the complete request path. Those are proposed checks.

Plan stakeholder involvement

I documented the sponsor, government IT, project roles, contractors, kiosk hosts and public user groups. I used interest, influence and expectations to plan the engagement. The activities move from workshops and design reviews to build demonstrations, testing and training.

  • Decision makers need scope, cost and milestone information.
  • Technical and site teams need specifications, access, approvals and installation coordination.
  • The plan calls for an issue register, minutes within 24 hours, monthly sponsor dashboards and engagement reviews at phase boundaries.

Connect integration, communication and change control

Our integration plan joins portal, kiosk, regional-server and database work. It proposes iterative development and a pilot before full rollout. Changes are logged, assessed with specialists, approved through the sponsor/steering process, and reflected in the affected plans.

  • Abesan’s communications plan includes monthly sponsor reports, weekly technical/vendor coordination, biweekly risk reporting and host training.
  • A critical issue triggers immediate escalation; an approved change needs a recorded decision and communication.

Follow the group schedule through handover

The detailed group schedule runs from January 1, 2026 through April 23, 2027. I use that detailed schedule as the planning basis here. It progresses through research, design, development/testing and launch/handover; these dates are scenario assumptions.

  • Initiation: 7 working days. Research: 79. Design/analysis: 133.
  • Development, implementation and testing: 105 working days. Launch/handover: 18.

Review the complete group budget

Our group phase budget totals CAD 4,343,966. Development, implementation and testing accounts for CAD 3,571,906. The resource mix is CAD 3,989,750 in materials and CAD 354,216 in work, so procurement assumptions drive most of the estimate.

  • The group budget is separate from my CAD 1,066,464 individual assignment.

Use a consistent earned-value example

The group’s cost exercise simulates a completed UI/UX design task with BAC, PV and EV of CAD 7,520. A hypothetical additional licence cost makes AC CAD 27,520. The corrected calculations show a task can be complete on its planned-value basis while remaining over budget.

  • CV = EV - AC = -CAD 20,000; CPI = 7,520 / 27,520 = 0.27.
  • SV = EV - PV = 0; SPI = 1.00.
  • For the completed task, EAC = CAD 27,520 and VAC = -CAD 20,000. This worked example is separate from the full kiosk budget.

Prioritize risks and assign owners

Our risk plan groups technology, procurement, financial, schedule and people risks. Integration failure and kiosk procurement delay receive the highest score of 9. The register assigns owners so a risk has an accountable response rather than only a description.

  • Technical risks: integration, LAN outage, cybersecurity and database compatibility.
  • Delivery risks: procurement, budget overrun, schedule/scope, weak requirements and stakeholder resistance.
  • Use consistent probability/impact bands when comparing the entries.

Plan responses, exposure and fallback options

The proposed responses include phased integration testing, middleware, specialist support and early vendor selection. A delivery problem could trigger a secondary supplier or an initial 150-kiosk rollout; unresolved integration could lead to a portal-first launch.

  • Five scenario probability-impact calculations total CAD 2,289,000 of expected monetary exposure; this is not an incurred loss or an automatic reserve amount.
  • Weekly checks, biweekly priority reviews and phase gates support monitoring.
  • A CPI below 0.90 or confirmed vendor delay is a proposed action trigger. Scope changes still require approval.

Prepare acceptance and operational handover

Our plan closes with validation, acceptance, documentation, training and lessons learned. The operational owner must be clear because ongoing maintenance is outside project scope. The handover therefore needs more than an installation-complete milestone.

  • Keep requirements, approvals and acceptance evidence connected.
  • Review residual risks and unresolved issues with their owners.
  • Use the same agreed schedule and budget basis when reporting status.

What I learned

  • Duration, work and cost measure different parts of a plan.
  • A complete group proposal needs connected requirements, scope, resources, risk and communication.
  • Use consistent scenario boundaries before interpreting a performance index.

Source: the full ITM750 portfolio supplied for this project. Evidence is from the original coursework; this edition adds no new lab test results. Repeated captures and earlier drafts are consolidated. Revised design summaries are labelled, and sensitive identifiers are masked.
